messages.author: af9de7b555d51702
messages.subject: Adaptive phase using runMCMC
parts:
Dear nimble group,

As I understand it, the runMCMC function automatically discards burn-in iterations. Are adaptation iterations automatically removed also? Or, does the resulting mcmc object still include the adaptive phase?

I attached a simple N-mixture model example if it helps. The simulation values are just to replicate the question. Thanks!

messages.author: c9e9cbbfb3b043f0
messages.subject: Re: Adaptive phase using runMCMC
parts:
Nathan, thanks for your interest in NIMBLE.  Let me explain how runMCMC(), and NIMBLE's MCMC samplers in general, operate.

For runMCMC(), you specify the arguments niter, and nburnin.  The default values are niter = 10,000 (total MCMC iterations to run), and burnin = 0 (by default no, burnin iterations are discarded).

The "adaptation" of most of NIMBLE's MCMC samplers operate using continuously decaying adaptation, not any finite adaptation period.  That is, they are "adapting" throughout the entire course of the MCMC, however the magnitude of the adaptation necessarily decays during the MCMC run.  So at first, the tuning parameters adapt a lot, then gradually less and less so.  In the extreme case, after say millions and millions of MCMC iterations, the adaptation (although present) would be negligible.

So, when you specify a burnin of, say nburnin = 1,000, the first 1,000 iterations will be discarded, and runMCMC() will return 9,000 MCMC samples.  For those samples returned, the samplers are still adapting, but much less so than in the initial 1,000 iterations that were discarded.  The default adaptation interval for most samplers is 200 iterations, so this would be discarding the first 5 (and most extreme) adaptive phases.

Does this make sense?  Does it answer your question?

Cheers,
Daniel
NIMBLE development team

messages.author: bebd85531a67ef86
messages.subject: Re: Adaptive phase using runMCMC
parts:
Nice question! There are Bayesian purists out there who are very against leaving adaptation on. My impression is that the main issue is a risk of non-stationarity in variance estimates and for this diagnostics tools can provide useful checks.

Inside runMCMC is a loop over your nchains that contains the line
mcmc$run(niter, progressBar = progressBar)
That means that the buildMCMC runtime parameter reset is taking on the default TRUE value for each chain, so the iteration counter used to slow down adaptation is being reset for each sampler.

Currently many of the samplers have an adaptive flag that can be set in the setup code. You could reset the value of this flag for each sampler in R with something like 
Rmcmc$samplerFunctions[[1]]$adaptive <- FALSE
but the equivelent in C
Cmcmc$samplerFunctions[[1]]$adaptive <- FALSE
does not seem to work, so you'd have to recompile - at which point you loose any adaptations obtained from previous MCMC runs.

To be able to toggle adaptation on/off within compiled C code would probably require that an adaptive run time argument is added to buildMCMC and that each sampler has a method function that can be called by buildMCMC's run code to toggle the sampler's adaptive arguments. Perhaps one for the To Do list?

Best
David

messages.author: c9e9cbbfb3b043f0
messages.subject: Re: Adaptive phase using runMCMC
parts:
Yes, there are several different points when you can change the frequency of the adaptation interval for adaptive samplers.  Most simply, this will affect all samplers in an MCMC, (see section 7.2.2.3 "Overriding the default sampler control list values" of the user manual), when you first call configureMCMC, provide the "control" argument, and specify the new adaptation interval, as:

mcmcConf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel, control = list(adaptInterval = 100))

This will make all adaptive MCMC samplers in that MCMC configuration use an adaptation interval of every-100-iterations, instead of the default value of every-200-iterations.  Advantage: adaptation will take place twice as often, and samplers may (in theory) approach their optimal mixing performance faster.  Disadvantages: more computation required for the adaptation procedures (as you mentioned; although this is essentially negligible for all univariate samplers, and only plays a real factor for multivariate samplers, for example the RW_block sampler), and also that each adaptation phase will be using *half as much information* on which to base its adaptation of internal parameters.  In contrast, the default of every-200-iterations will (in theory) make "more educated" adaptations, albeit half as often, because it's using the information from the most recent 200 iterations for its calculations.  But it's an open question in what situations larger or smaller adaptation intervals are preferable, and certainly is case dependent.

You can also change the adaptation interval of individual samplers, by adding them to the MCMC configuration, as:

conf$addSampler(type = SAMPLERTYPE, target = NODE, adaptInterval = 100)

Good questions, keep at it,
Daniel
